item.title: Keenetic / NetCraze
item.description:
keen-pbr can be installed on Keenetic / NetCraze routers via Entware ’s opkg package manager.

Install Entware on the router

First, ensure that Entware is installed on your router. Please consult the official router manual for Keenetic or NetCraze:

  1. Find your router’s manual.
  2. In the search field, search for “Installing the Entware repository on a USB drive”.
  3. Read and follow the instructions carefully.

Install required components

Open your router’s configuration page, navigate to Management -> System settings, and install the following additional components:

  • Network Functions / IPv6 Protocol (On NDMS 5.0+ is absent because it is a part of core now)
  • OPKG Packages / Open Package System Support
  • OPKG Packages / Netfilter Subsystem Kernel Modules
  • OPKG Packages / Xtables-addons Extension Package for Netfilter
  • Utilities and services / DNS-over-TLS proxy (optional, but highly recommended)
  • Utilities and services / DNS-over-HTTPS proxy (optional, but highly recommended)

Configure DoH/DoT on the router

It is recommended to set up DoH /DoT DNS servers on your router to protect yourself from DNS spoofing attacks.

Consult the official Keenetic documentation on how to do it: DoH and DoT proxy servers for DNS requests encryption.

Install keen-pbr from the repository

  1. Open keen-pbr repository page.
  2. Select “Keenetic / NetCraze” in the OS selector on the left, choose the “current” version, and select the architecture that matches your router.
    • TIP: You can run opkg print-architecture in an SSH session to see your router’s architecture.
  3. Follow the instructions on the repository page carefully.
  4. Run the opkg install keen-pbr command.
    • Example install command:
      bash
      opkg install keen-pbr

# or if you want headless version (without API and without WebUI)
# opkg install keen-pbr-headless

Ensure that keen-pbr service is up and running

Before continuing to the next step, it is recommended to check whether keen-pbr started successfully and has not crashed. Run /opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr status. If it is dead, see Troubleshooting.

Example:

~ # /opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr status
 Checking keen-pbr...              alive.

If the service is alive, continue to the next step.

Configure the service

Open http://my.keenetic.net:12121 to configure keen-pbr (if you installed the full version; the headless version does not provide a Web UI).

You can also configure keen-pbr manually by modifying the configuration file: /opt/etc/keen-pbr/config.json.

Choose RAW or mangle PREROUTING

This choice exists only on Keenetic / NetCraze. keen-pbr sets fwmark in one of two firewall tables:

  • ** mangle **: Keenetic rebuilds this table from time to time (for example after a DHCP lease renewal), and keen-pbr’s rules are briefly missing until keen-pbr restores them;
  • raw: Keenetic does not touch it, but rules from Connection Policies > Policy Bindings run later and overwrite keen-pbr’s fwmark.

See also the Keenetic Community forum thread about Keenetic rebuilding iptables.

Mode Benefit Trade-off
RAW (default when available) PBR remains active across a Keenetic mangle rebuild. Long-running, sensitive flows such as gaming sessions avoid rebuild-related breaks, and packets have fewer chances to bypass the VPN. After keen-pbr sets its fwmark in RAW, Keenetic’s Connection Policies > Policy Bindings rules overwrite it. RAW mode therefore works only for devices assigned the Default policy.
mangle keen-pbr runs after Keenetic sets its own fwmarks for Connection Policy, so it can override routing for devices with a non-default policy. When Keenetic rebuilds its mangle table (usually about every five minutes), keen-pbr rules disappear briefly. A few packets can use the ordinary route before keen-pbr restores them, disrupting a gaming session or another sensitive flow.
For the most predictable Keenetic setup, do not assign Connection Policies to devices in Keenetic. Instead, create the equivalent per-device keen-pbr route rules using the src_addr (Source address) field. This keeps routing policy in keen-pbr and avoids conflicts with Keenetic policy bindings.

By default keen-pbr checks separately for IPv4 and IPv6 whether RAW is available, and uses it if so; otherwise mangle. The system log shows the selected mode after the service starts:

IPv4 raw PREROUTING available
WARNING: IPv6 raw PREROUTING unavailable: ...

To always use mangle, add this line to /opt/etc/keen-pbr/defaults:

KEEN_PBR_RAW_PREROUTING="disable"

and restart the service:

/opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr restart

The other values of this variable are described in CLI.

Basic commands:

Action Command
Start service /opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr start
Restart service /opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr restart
Check if keen-pbr alive /opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr status
If you do not plan to use the keen-pbr Web UI or API, consider installing the keen-pbr-headless package. It uses less storage space (~1.2 MB instead of ~2.8 MB) and does not include the API server at all. You can also disable the API server at any time via a config flag, even when using the full package version.

Next steps

Go to the Quick Start page and use the Web UI tab for the easiest initial setup. If you installed the headless version, see the JSON / CLI tab instead.

Separate DNS servers for lists (dnsmasq)

keen-pbr does not need dnsmasq for routing. Install it only if you want to send the domains of some lists to separate DNS servers, or set your own default DNS servers. See Do I need dnsmasq?.

Install dnsmasq

  1. Install the package over SSH. Entware has only dnsmasq-full; the name dnsmasq resolves to it:
    bash
    opkg install dnsmasq-full
  2. To apply the recommended dnsmasq settings, run this over SSH:
    bash
    /opt/usr/lib/keen-pbr/dnsmasq-hook.sh install-recommended-config
    It replaces /opt/etc/dnsmasq.conf and saves the previous file as /opt/etc/dnsmasq.conf.backup-keenpbr. my.keenetic.net keeps resolving.
  3. Open http://my.keenetic.net/a (if the link does not open, use http://<router-ip>/a) and run: 
    opkg dns-override
system configuration save
    Run these commands only after dnsmasq is installed. Without dnsmasq, dns-override leaves the LAN without DNS.
  4. Reboot the router. This is required: without a reboot LAN clients keep using the built-in DNS proxy, and dnsmasq does not get their queries.
  5. In the Web UI, open General > Local DNS server management and turn on Manage dnsmasq configuration. The DNS servers and DNS rules pages become available.

Return to how it was

Do the steps in this order, so the LAN keeps DNS all the time:

  1. In the Web UI, turn off Manage dnsmasq configuration (General > Local DNS server management) and apply the config. dnsmasq keeps running and uses the servers from /opt/etc/keen-pbr/dnsmasq-fallback.conf, so DNS keeps working. If dnsmasq has servers of its own, these are added to them; clear the file to avoid that.
  2. In the web CLI (http://my.keenetic.net/a) run: 
    no opkg dns-override
system configuration save
  3. Reboot the router. This is required.
  4. Remove the package:
    bash
    opkg remove dnsmasq-full

To keep dnsmasq with its previous settings after install-recommended-config, put the saved file back instead of removing the package:

bash
cp /opt/etc/dnsmasq.conf.backup-keenpbr /opt/etc/dnsmasq.conf
/opt/etc/init.d/S56dnsmasq restart

item.title: OpenWrt
item.description:
keen-pbr can be installed on OpenWrt routers from the keen-pbr package repository.

Check which package manager your OpenWrt version uses

The repository page automatically shows the correct flow for your target:

  • OpenWrt 25.x and newer: apk
  • OpenWrt 24.x and older: opkg

Install from the repository page

Open the repository instructions page, select OpenWrt in the OS selector on the left, and use the generated commands for your exact version and architecture:

keen-pbr repository

Example install commands:

bash
# OpenWrt 25.x and newer
apk update
apk add keen-pbr

# or if you want headless version (without API and without WebUI)
# apk update
# apk add keen-pbr-headless
bash
# OpenWrt 24.x and older
opkg update
opkg install keen-pbr

# or if you want headless version (without API and without WebUI)
# opkg update
# opkg install keen-pbr-headless

The package installs its config at /etc/keen-pbr/config.json and enables the init script automatically.

Useful service commands:

bash
service keen-pbr start
service keen-pbr enable
service keen-pbr restart
If you do not plan to use the keen-pbr Web UI or API, you can install the keen-pbr-headless package instead. It uses less storage space (~1.2 MB instead of ~2.8 MB) and does not include the API server at all. Also, you can disable API server via config flag at any time on the full package version.
DNS and L7 interception needs the kernel modules nfnetlink_queue, nfnetlink_log and nft_queue. The package pulls in kmod-nfnetlink-queue, kmod-nfnetlink-log and kmod-nft-queue automatically. If you installed an older build or removed them, install them manually; otherwise the daemon logs cannot bind netfilter queue/log ... Invalid argument and /api/health/service names the missing module. nft_log is part of kmod-nft-core.

Next steps

Open Quick Start and use the Web UI tab for the easiest first setup. If you installed keen-pbr-headless, use the JSON / CLI tab instead.

If pre-built packages are not yet available for your platform, see Build from Source to compile keen-pbr yourself.

Separate DNS servers for lists (dnsmasq)

keen-pbr does not need dnsmasq for routing, but OpenWrt already uses it as the system resolver. See Do I need dnsmasq? to decide whether you want keen-pbr to manage it.

Turn it on

In the Web UI, open General > Local DNS server management and turn on Manage dnsmasq configuration. keen-pbr adds three addnmount entries to the dnsmasq section in /etc/config/dhcp, so that the sandboxed dnsmasq can run keen-pbr.

While management is on and Default DNS servers are set, keen-pbr takes the servers without a domain out of the list in /etc/config/dhcp (LuCI DNS forwardings). Per-domain servers such as /lan/192.168.1.1 stay. The removed servers return when you turn management off or clear the default servers.

Return to how it was

Turn off Manage dnsmasq configuration and apply the config. keen-pbr restarts dnsmasq and returns the removed servers. Removing the package also removes the addnmount entries it added.

item.title: Debian
item.description:
keen-pbr can be installed on Debian systems from the keen-pbr APT repository.

Add the repository from the repository page

Open the repository instructions page, select Debian in the OS selector on the left, and use the generated commands for your release and architecture:

keen-pbr repository

The generated instructions include the signing key and the apt source entry.

Install the package

Example install command:

bash
apt update
apt install keen-pbr

# or if you want headless version (without API and without WebUI)
# apt update
# apt install keen-pbr-headless

The package installs its config at /etc/keen-pbr/config.json and enables the systemd service automatically.

Useful service commands:

bash
systemctl start keen-pbr
systemctl status keen-pbr
systemctl restart keen-pbr
If you do not plan to use the keen-pbr Web UI or API, the keen-pbr-headless package uses less storage space (~1.2 MB instead of ~2.8 MB) and does not include the API server at all. Also, you can disable API server via config flag at any time on the full package version.

Next steps

Open Quick Start and use the Web UI tab for the easiest first setup. If you installed keen-pbr-headless, use the JSON / CLI tab instead.

If pre-built packages are not yet available for your platform, see Build from Source to compile keen-pbr yourself.

Separate DNS servers for lists (dnsmasq)

keen-pbr does not need dnsmasq for routing. Install it only if you want separate DNS servers for some lists or your own default DNS servers. See Do I need dnsmasq?.

Install dnsmasq

bash
apt install dnsmasq

To apply the recommended dnsmasq settings, run:

bash
/usr/lib/keen-pbr/dnsmasq-hook.sh install-recommended-config

It replaces /etc/dnsmasq.conf and saves the previous file as /etc/dnsmasq.conf.backup-keenpbr. dnsmasq then answers only your local networks and takes its servers from keen-pbr.

Then, in the Web UI, open General > Local DNS server management and turn on Manage dnsmasq configuration. keen-pbr adds a marked block to /etc/dnsmasq.conf; the recommended config already has it. Point the system resolver (or your DHCP server) at dnsmasq if it is not already used.

Return to how it was

  1. Turn off Manage dnsmasq configuration and apply the config. dnsmasq restarts and uses the servers from /etc/keen-pbr/dnsmasq-fallback.conf. If dnsmasq has servers of its own, these are added to them; clear the file to avoid that.
  2. Restore the system resolver you used before dnsmasq.
  3. If you ran install-recommended-config, put the old settings back:
    bash
    cp /etc/dnsmasq.conf.backup-keenpbr /etc/dnsmasq.conf
systemctl restart dnsmasq
  4. Or remove the package:
    bash
    apt remove dnsmasq
